heading: Many MLP neurons in transformer language models fire on unrelated inputs, varying by layer
definition: a large share of MLP neurons in transformer language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, more in some layers than others.
summary: Groups independent of the original authors report polysemantic MLP neurons in GPT-2, Pythia, Gemma, Llama and Qwen models, so the neurons are known to exist across model families. No random-sample estimate shows that they are a large share, the two measured shares of polysemantic neurons disagree, and studies disagree on which layers have the most.

suggested_status.by_scale: toy: no studies (counts versions.V2.studies_by_size has no toy key). <1B: R2 for existence (GPT2-small in 2211.12312 and lw:QwgYmpnMxBZnmGCsw; Pythia 70M in 2305.01610 is same-group, so R1). The only share counted at this size is below 5% per layer under an SAE-connection criterion: top 3 neurons per 0.4-cosine SAE feature cluster, connection >0.2 (2505.11611, stated jointly for Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small). 1-10B: R2 for existence across GPT-2 XL, Pythia 1B (same-group, 2305.01610), Gemma-2-2b, Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.1 8B, from several groups; the layer trend is contested. 10-100B: R2 for existence, from two studies on two families: one Pythia-12B neuron (2402.01702#R3) and Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct (2511.06739#r1). The share part is not supported by a count from a random sample with an activation-based criterion. The only share counted at this size is 46.9% polysemantic, 32.9% fuzzy and 20.2% monosemantic (2511.06739; the first 60 neurons of each MLP rather than a random sample; gpt-5-mini on top-64 contexts, one judge). That is R0 at most for the share part, and the count awaits a re-check of its classes, which its record still swaps (only the check's reading of Figure 1 (left) corrects them). The layer part is untested at this size because there is no per-layer data. >100B: no stated sizes; the Claude 3 Sonnet size is not stated, and both Claude 3 Sonnet records are same-group.
suggested_status.reason: Polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer LMs are reported, mostly qualitatively, on GPT-2 (2309.10312, 2506.15538, 2211.12312), Pythia (2305.01610, 2402.01702, 2503.23298), Gemma (2502.16994, 2610.24521), Llama (2502.16994#R17), Qwen (2511.06739) and Claude 3 Sonnet (web scaling-monosemanticity, the same work as arXiv:2605.29358). Author overlap: counts: versions.V2.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 2. The studies index marks arXiv:2305.01610 and arXiv:2605.29358 SAME GROUP, and their author lists share names with an original, so these are the two. The web Scaling Monosemanticity record has no flag in the index, but as the same work it inherits 2605.29358's flag. The Pythia evidence of 2305.01610 and all Claude 3 Sonnet evidence are therefore R1 (same-group), not independent. 2610.24521's author list shares no name with an original. Its check notes Anthropic-affiliated authors, an affiliation-only case left to Iris. Verdict counts: versions.V2.verdicts.supports.studies = 13, limits_scope.studies = 6, challenges.studies = 0. These counts were built before the checks and have not been rebuilt. limits_scope.studies still includes 2511.06739, whose V2 verdict the check corrects to supports. versions.V2.rows_by_state still counts lw:JA5Eyf2cqyL3HbKxS#r1 as observed, which the check reads as partial at most for V2, and 2511.06739#r1 as partial, which the check reads as observed. No corrected totals are given here. For the 'large share' part, no study counts a share of randomly sampled MLP neurons with an activation-based criterion. The two counted shares use different definitions and disagree. Under an SAE-connection criterion, fewer than 5% of neurons per layer are polysemantic in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small (2505.11611). In Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct, a gpt-5-mini judge on the top-64 contexts of the first 60 neurons of each MLP rates 46.9% polysemantic and 32.9% fuzzy (2511.06739). That is one judge on one model, not a random sample, and its record still swaps the polysemantic and monosemantic classes; only the check corrects them, and that fix has not reached the record. Random Claude 3 Sonnet neurons 'typically' fire in multiple unrelated contexts, but no numbers are given, and the work is same-group. The layer part rests on proxies that disagree: early layers in a weight statistic (2305.01610, same-group), middle layers in FKR and Purity (2503.23298, 2502.16994), and no consistent trend (2506.15538). 2511.06739 gives no per-layer data. R2 therefore fits only the existence of such neurons across families, which groups other than the originals' report at <1B, 1-10B and 10-100B. The 'large share' part is not supported by a count from a random sample of MLP neurons with an activation-based criterion. The random-sample evidence gives no share. Claude 3 Sonnet neurons are compared with SAE features only qualitatively or by significance (same-group, R1). A manual inspection of 50 randomly sampled layer-12 Gemma-2-2b neurons found high polysemanticity (2502.16994, another group; text, not a row). 2506.15538 gives mean PRISM scores for 20 randomly chosen neurons per layer, with no threshold or prevalence estimate (figure only). 2610.24521 runs a cluster sort eval on 50 random Gemma 3 4B L22 neurons (not in rows; whether it is same-group is left to Iris). The one count that points to a large share is a single judge-based count whose classes await a re-check. The layer part is not settled.
suggested_status.open_questions: Three results would sharpen the level. First, a share of randomly sampled MLP neurons with an activation-based criterion over the full activation range, reported per layer in two or more families, from a group other than the originals'; this would give the 'large share' part a random-sample number. Second, a numeric version of the Claude 3 Sonnet neuron-vs-feature comparison; as same-group work it would extend the share part at R1, not reproduce it. Third, an early-vs-middle layer comparison on the same Pythia models with one metric. Also open: a re-check of 2511.06739's classes against its Figure 1 (left), since its record still swaps the polysemantic and monosemantic classes and only the check corrects them. Even if the 46.9% holds, it does not come from a random sample, so the first result above is still what would give 'large share' a random-sample number. Also open: whether the 46.9% judge-based share in Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct holds under another judge or prompt, beyond the first 60 neurons per MLP, and per layer; and whether the SAE-connection criterion of 2505.11611 and an LLM-judge criterion give different shares on the same model. Still open, for Iris: whether 2610.24521 counts as same-group (its check notes Anthropic-affiliated authors; no shared name). If it does, 1-10B existence still rests on 2309.10312, 2506.15538 and 2502.16994. Also open: whether shares differ with training stage or above 100B. The quoted verdict counts need re-quoting once the checks' fixes (2511.06739's verdict and its r1 state, lw:JA5Eyf2cqyL3HbKxS#r1's state) reach the records and the counts are rebuilt.

source.title: Softmax Linear Units
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Neel Nanda; Tom Henighan; Scott Johnston; Sheer El Showk; Nicholas Joseph; Nova DasSarma; Ben Mann; Danny Hernandez; Amanda Askell; Kamal Ndousse; Andy Jones; Dawn Drain; Anna Chen; Yuntao Bai; Deep Ganguli; Liane Lovitt; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; Jackson Kernion; Tom Conerly; Shauna Kravec; Stanislav Fort; Saurav Kadavath; Josh Jacobson; Eli Tran-Johnson; Jared Kaplan; Jack Clark; Tom Brown; Sam McCandlish; Dario Amodei; Christopher Olah

original_result.setup: Blinded raters judged the top-activating examples of 60 neurons per model and marked a neuron interpretable if one rule explained 80% of its strongest firings.
original_result.result: About 35% of neurons in baseline transformers of 1 to 40 layers were rated interpretable. The rating does not separate polysemantic neurons from other uninterpretable ones, and it gives no breakdown by layer.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: GPT-2 MLP neurons looked highly polysemantic; one fired on commas, diminutive adjectives and prepositions.
Early-layer Pythia neurons probe-selected for specific n-grams fired on many unrelated n-grams in a wider corpus.
About 38% of the most salient Gemma-2-2B residual-stream dimensions were shared across all part-of-speech classes.
Human raters and PRISM, a multi-concept description method, found distinct concepts in one GPT-2 XL neuron.
A proxy polysemanticity score was higher in Pythia's middle layers than in top and bottom layers.
Gemma 3 4B neurons trailed transcoder features over broad activation ranges; one mixed several concepts.
Most inspected errors in automatic GPT-2 XL neuron explanations reflected neurons mixing unrelated coherent concepts.
One Pythia-12B neuron responded to apparently unrelated triggers even at its highest activations.
Example GPT-2 neurons fired strongly on random text semantically far from their top-activating inputs.
Gemma-2-2b layer-12 MLP neurons were highly polysemantic, with the lowest purity (concept-specific firing) among tested layers.
Randomly sampled Claude 3 Sonnet MLP neurons typically fired in multiple unrelated contexts.
Most top-ranked GPT2-small neurons for an Odyssey passage did not match it or were highly polysemantic.
Manual inspection found sampled Claude 3 Sonnet neurons typically active in multiple unrelated contexts.
GPT-2 XL and Llama 3.1 8B neuron polysemanticity showed no consistent layer trend.
Under a strict test using sparse autoencoders, fewer than 5% of neurons per layer were polysemantic.
At peak activations, Gemma 3 4B neurons matched transcoder features (sparse MLP replacements) in interpretability.
Inspected GPT-2 XL neurons looked like unitary abstract concepts, not unrelated mixtures.
Above activation 5, a Pythia-12B neuron responded almost only to example-related phrases.
An LLM judge (gpt-5-mini) rated 46.9% of sampled Qwen-2.5-32B neurons polysemantic and 20.2% monosemantic.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.basis: counts: versions.V2.studies_by_size has only the keys 'not stated' (10), '1-10B' (8), '<1B' (3) and '10-100B' (2). The Claude 3 Sonnet rows give no size (web#R1: 'not stated').

untested.what: A share of polysemantic MLP neurons counted per layer, with a contrast between layers in one model. Layer evidence exists only as proxies (FKR, Purity, weight statistics, mean PRISM scores).
untested.basis: Untested-parts lines: 2505.11611 (no layer-by-layer contrast reported), 2511.06739 (no per-layer breakdown), 2610.24521 (layer dependence only hypothesised), 2305.01610 (weight-statistic proxy), 2506.15538 (no threshold or prevalence estimate). counts: versions.V2.main_rows_by_operation has only measurement (61) and evaluation (4).

untested.what: A share of randomly sampled MLP neurons that respond to unrelated inputs, scored over the full activation range rather than only top examples or SAE connections.
untested.basis: 2511.06739 counts a share only from the top-64 contexts of the first 60 neurons of each MLP in Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct, classified by gpt-5-mini: 46.9% polysemantic, 32.9% fuzzy, 20.2% monosemantic (arXiv:2511.06739#r1, Figure 1 left; classes as corrected by the checks, since r1's note and verdict fix swap them). 2505.11611 is not activation-based: it counts connections between SAE features and neurons (connection >0.2), per its untested-parts line. The Claude 3 Sonnet records give no numbers. The original's measure is 'not interpretable at first glance' on top examples, per its untested-parts line. counts: versions.V2.rows_by_state.cannot_determine = 31 of versions.V2.rows_linked = 65.

untested.what: Whether the share changes with training stage (base vs instruct or fine-tuned) within one model.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V2.studies_by_stage shows base 9, instruct/chat 3, fine-tuned 2, other 1, not stated 7, but no pack row varies stage within a model.

wording_issues.issue: The statement gives no number for 'large', and the two counted shares differ widely with the definition used. Under an SAE-connection criterion, fewer than 5% of neurons in each layer count as polysemantic neurons with strong connections. The criterion takes the top 3 neurons per 0.4-cosine SAE feature cluster and keeps connections above 0.2. The figure is stated jointly for Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small (2505.11611#r1, r2). In Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct, gpt-5-mini classified the first 60 neurons of each MLP from their top-64 contexts: 46.9% polysemantic, 32.9% fuzzy and 20.2% monosemantic (2511.06739#r1, Figure 1 left; pooled, no per-layer breakdown). That near-half share comes from one LLM judge on one model. The Claude 3 Sonnet study says sampled neurons 'typically' fire in multiple unrelated contexts but gives no numbers. The original's baseline measure (~35% interpretable at first glance, 1L-40L) does not separate polysemantic neurons from neurons that are uninterpretable for other reasons, per its own untested-parts line.

wording_issues.phrase: more in some layers than others
wording_issues.issue: The layer evidence rests on proxies, and these disagree on direction. Early layers stand out in Pythia weight statistics (2305.01610). Middle layers stand out in Pythia FKR (2503.23298) and in Gemma-2-2b layer-12 Purity of 0.43 (2502.16994). GPT-2 XL and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct show no consistent trend (2506.15538).

Several results describe the extra activations as coherent concepts, not random ones. In GPT-2 XL, the authors inspected 100 explanations with Type II errors. Most error cases were inputs unrelated to the explanation that formed coherent concepts of their own (2309.10312#R3). The lw post's author says they have not really encountered GPT-2 XL neurons that mix unrelated concepts, and reads the neurons as unitary abstract concepts. In footnote 2, a food-porn neuron fires on erotic stories and cooking instructions. The author calls these 'decently unrelated' but united by a hedonic theme (lw:JA5Eyf2cqyL3HbKxS#r1). The post gives no sample, layers or method. The row's 'observed' state fits V6. For V2 the check reads it as partial at most, in line with the V2 limits_scope verdict. The Gemma-2-2B overlap is across labelled classes such as POS and DBpedia, not unrelated tokens (2508.15094 untested-parts line).
Some supporting units are not MLP neurons. 2508.15094 measures residual-stream hidden-state dimensions, per its verdict fix. 2505.11611 states no restriction to MLP neurons.

Whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs depends on the activation range examined. Pythia-12B L10.N5 is near-specific above activation 5. Gemma 3 4B L22 neurons match transcoder features under top sampling but degrade under quantile sampling.

method_sensitivity.what: Gemma 3 4B L22: neuron sort-eval scores are comparable to transcoder features under top sampling (R1) but degrade noticeably under quantile sampling (R2). Pythia-12B L10.N5 is near-specific above activation 5 and called polysemantic only below it (R2), while L3.N1000 is polysemantic even at its highest activations (R3). In 2506.15538, description quality changes with the activation-percentile interval. The original's caveat: top dataset examples show monosemanticity only when a neuron activates strongly (E3).

An SAE-connection criterion (top 3 neurons per SAE feature cluster, connection >0.2, cluster cutoff cosine 0.4) gives fewer than 5% polysemantic neurons per layer in Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small (2505.11611). An LLM three-way classification of Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct MLP neurons (first 60 per MLP, gpt-5-mini on top-64 contexts) gives 46.9% polysemantic, 32.9% fuzzy and 20.2% monosemantic (2511.06739#r1, Figure 1 left). That study uses one judge and one classification prompt and compares no definitions. The two counts also differ in model, units and sampling, so the contrast is between studies, not a within-study test. 2508.15094 says binary top-80 overlap counts a unit as shared even when its concept-conditioned distributions separate, and such units may still count as monosemantic. Its three measures (top-80 overlap, all-active SAE overlap, Jensen-Shannon separability) agree in direction: SAEs below base, the 65k SAE below the 16k. No share of polysemantic units is compared across definitions.

method_sensitivity.factor: rater, description method and scoring metric
method_sensitivity.what: In the original (Section 6.2), one annotator rated about 20% of baseline neurons and about 60% of SoLU neurons interpretable. The other two rated about 40% (baseline) and about 60% (SoLU), so the raters differ only on baseline neurons (R5). After unblinding, the authors' sense was that this annotator held a higher bar and was less willing to ignore small activations, and they hesitate to draw a strong inference from it. 2410.16443 reports that GPT-2 vs CRATE vs GPT2-SAE rankings change with the metric. In 2502.16994, Purity changes with the description method (feature 5183). 2309.10312 reports that observational and intervention evaluations differ.

method_sensitivity.factor: feature or probe dataset and corpus
method_sensitivity.what: In 2503.23298, FKR and the reliability of the analysis change with the feature dataset; sparse probing on Code Language is anomalous for Pythia 70M. In 2305.01610, interpretation depends on the probe dataset, the feature definition, the corpus used to inspect activations, and summary metrics versus raw activation counts. In 2508.15094, results vary with dataset, SAE width and l0.

Gemma-2-2b Purity is 0.55, 0.43, 0.61 and 0.54 at layers 3, 12, 20 and 25 (2502.16994). GPT2-SMALL Odyssey match counts are 17 in layer 0 and 3 in layers 10 and 11, without denominators (lw:QwgYmpnMxBZnmGCsw). In 2506.15538, polysemanticity scores vary across models and feature types. In 2503.23298, FKR varies with model scale and layer. In the original, the SoLU gain at 64 layers is only 33% to 42%.

status_amendment.public_note: Two studies, 'Finding Neurons in a Haystack' (Pythia models) and the Claude 3 Sonnet study, are now marked as work by the original authors' group, and no count from a random sample of neurons yet supports the 'large share' part (the one count pointing that way, 46.9% of the neurons checked in Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct as judged by a single AI model, still needs its categories re-checked). The level is unchanged at R2, which covers only the existence of such neurons across model families, not how common they are or which layers have more.
